content: A pregnancy test is a diagnostic tool used to determine whether a woman is pregnant. The earliest form of pregnancy testing involves the detection of Early Pregnancy Factor (EPF) through a rosette inhibition assay. EPF can be identified in the blood within 48 hours of fertilization. However, testing for EPF is both costly and time-intensive. Modern chemical pregnancy tests primarily detect the presence of the beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) in blood or urine. hCG becomes detectable after implantation, which typically occurs 6 to 12 days following fertilization. Quantitative blood tests, also known as serum beta hCG tests, can detect hCG levels as low as 1 mIU/mL. In contrast, urine-based tests have detection thresholds ranging from 20 mIU/mL to 100 mIU/mL, depending on the brand. Qualitative blood tests generally have a threshold of 25 mIU/mL, making them less sensitive than some home pregnancy tests. Obstetric ultrasonography can sometimes visualize the gestational sac as early as 4.5 weeks of gestation (approximately 2.5 weeks after ovulation). The yolk sac becomes visible around 5 weeks of gestation, and the embryo can be observed and measured by approximately 5.5 weeks. Cardiac activity, or the fetal heartbeat, may be detected as early as 6 weeks and is typically visible by 7 weeks of gestation. Historically, ancient Egyptians used a method where they watered bags of wheat and barley with the urine of a potentially pregnant woman. Germination indicated pregnancy, and the type of grain that sprouted was believed to predict the fetus's gender. Hippocrates suggested that a woman who missed her period should drink a solution of honey in water before bed; abdominal distension and cramps the following day were thought to indicate pregnancy. During the Middle Ages, Avicenna and other physicians practiced uroscopy, a nonscientific method of analyzing urine. In 1928, Selmar Aschheim and Bernhard Zondek introduced a test based on the detection of hCG. Their method involved injecting the urine of the test subject into an immature female mouse. The mouse was later dissected to check for ovulation, which indicated the presence of hCG and confirmed pregnancy. A similar test, known as the rabbit test, used immature rabbits and also required the animal to be sacrificed to examine its ovaries. An improvement came with the frog test, which was still in use during the 1950s. In this test, a female frog was injected with the patient’s serum or urine, and if the frog produced eggs within 24 hours, the test was positive. Unlike the mouse and rabbit tests, the frog remained alive and could be reused. Modern pregnancy test kits are designed to detect hCG in urine and provide a visual, qualitative result for early pregnancy detection at home. Records of pregnancy testing date back to ancient Greek and Egyptian cultures. False-negative results can occur if testing is performed too early. Quantitative blood tests and the most sensitive urine tests can detect hCG shortly after implantation, which occurs 6 to 12 days after ovulation. Less sensitive urine tests and qualitative blood tests may not detect pregnancy until 3 to 4 days after implantation. Since menstruation typically occurs 14 days after ovulation, the likelihood of a false-negative result decreases once a menstrual period is late. However, ovulation may not always occur at a predictable time in the menstrual cycle, and factors such as early or late ovulation can affect the timing of implantation and hCG detection. Using ovulation predictor kits (OPKs) or tracking fertility signs such as cervical mucus or basal body temperature can provide a more accurate indication of when to test than relying on day-counting alone. The accuracy of a pregnancy test is more closely related to the day of ovulation rather than the day of intercourse. Sperm can survive in the fallopian tubes for up to five days, waiting for ovulation to occur. Implantation can take up to 12 additional days, meaning even the most sensitive pregnancy tests may yield false negatives up to 17 days after the act of intercourse that resulted in pregnancy. Some home pregnancy tests have high hCG detection thresholds (up to 100 mIU/mL), which may delay detection by an additional 3 to 4 days, potentially leading to false negatives up to three weeks after conception. False-positive results can occur due to evaporation lines on home pregnancy tests if the test is read outside the recommended 3–5 minute reaction window. It is essential to interpret the test within the time frame specified by the manufacturer. Women who have received an hCG injection as part of infertility treatment will test positive on pregnancy tests regardless of their actual pregnancy status. However, common infertility drugs like Clomid do not contain hCG. When used as directed by women who have not received an hCG injection, false-positive results are rare. Certain medical conditions, such as some cancers (e.g., lung cancer), can also cause elevated hCG levels. Pregnancy tests can also be used to assess the viability of a pregnancy. Serial quantitative blood tests, typically performed 2–3 days apart, can monitor hCG levels. Below an hCG level of 1,200 mIU/mL, hCG usually doubles every 48–72 hours, though a rise of 50–60% is still considered normal. Between 1,200 and 6,000 mIU/mL, hCG doubling time extends to 72–96 hours, and above 6,000 mIU/mL, it may take more than four days to double. Failure of hCG levels to rise appropriately may indicate an increased risk of miscarriage or a possible ectopic pregnancy. Ultrasound is another common tool for assessing pregnancy viability. Findings such as a lower-than-expected fetal heart rate or missed developmental milestones may suggest a problem with the pregnancy. However, a diagnosis should not be made based on a single ultrasound. Inaccurate estimations of fetal age and inherent limitations of ultrasound imaging can lead to misinterpretation. If the initial ultrasound suggests a problem, repeating the scan 7–10 days later is a reasonable approach.
